properties.title: PSI-102_Reports_SAME_Final Science Report.pdf
properties.summary: The report finds material-dependent smoke size distributions and different responses from ISS light-scattering and Shuttle ionization detectors. Silicone and lampwick produced a broader large-particle contribution than Kapton and Teflon under the described conditions. The recovered TEM grids were contaminated, limiting interpretation of microscopy. The closing discussion proposes size-discriminating or multiple-moment detection rather than inferring universal performance from a single detector response.

properties.title: SAME: material-dependent smoke sizes and diagnostics
properties.summary: The report finds material-dependent smoke size distributions and different responses from ISS light-scattering and Shuttle ionization detectors. Silicone and lampwick produced a broader large-particle contribution than Kapton and Teflon under the described conditions. The recovered TEM grids were contaminated, limiting interpretation of microscopy. The closing discussion proposes size-discriminating or multiple-moment detection rather than inferring universal performance from a single detector response.

evidence.locator: metadata.objective
evidence.text: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.

evidence.locator: metadata.approach
evidence.text: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
